design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD42016035486) of health outcomes associated with crack use, organized by ICD-10 chapter. Six databases (Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, LILACS), searched October 2015 and updated October 2016, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed case-control, cohort and cross-sectional studies with an explicit crack group (crack, freebase or alkaloid cocaine, or smoked cocaine; mixed groups if at least 75% used crack) and a comparison group not using crack or using it at different levels; no language or date limits. 302 articles were included from 4,700 records screened; 79 entered 24 meta-analyses (28 pooled estimates in Table 2), each comparing crack use with no crack use within the studies' populations, with controls described as non-drug-using or general-population; the rest were synthesized narratively. Evidence for selected outcomes was graded A (conclusive) to E (insufficient) by an approach described as GRADE. Comparisons of crack with powder or other cocaine use appear only in the narrative synthesis and are not tested. Read as the accepted manuscript: an unedited version with 81 numbered pages after a cover page.
can_establish: Which health outcomes had been studied in relation to crack use up to October 2016, in which populations, and the average, mostly crude, association between crack use and HIV, hepatitis C, sexually transmitted infections, mental-health problems, maternal and neonatal outcomes, and experienced violence, against people not using crack in the same studies.
cannot_establish: That crack use causes any of these outcomes (most pooled odds ratios are crude, from cross-sectional studies of high-risk populations, and the authors say crack is not a plausible direct cause of infections or violence); any difference between crack and powder cocaine (the meta-analyses compare crack use with no use, and crack–other-cocaine comparisons are only described narratively, as mixed); absolute risks (none are reported); or mortality, respiratory or cardiovascular risk with any precision (no pooling; those results are in an unread supplement and in Table 3).

sample.recruitment: Database search of Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO and LILACS in October 2015, updated October 2016, with hand-searching of reference lists; peer-reviewed publications only, for resource reasons; no language or publication-date limits (pp. 5–7 of the accepted manuscript).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case-control, cohort or cross-sectional design; an explicit crack group; a comparison group of people not using crack or at different levels of crack use; a health outcome measurable or diagnosable compatibly with ICD-10 from records, tests or self-report; quantitative risk estimates or data to compute odds ratios. Excluded: reviews and editorials, animal studies, unpublished or non-peer-reviewed work. Crack use meant crack, freebase or alkaloid cocaine, or smoked cocaine; mixed groups were included if at least 75% used crack (pp. 6–7 of the accepted manuscript). Meta-analyses required at least three studies with comparable control groups of people not using drugs or the general population (p. 8).
sample.demographics: Included articles: US 206 (68.2%), Brazil 32 (10.6%), Canada 22 (7.3%), the rest from Central and South America, Europe, Asia and Africa; 203 cross-sectional or cohort-baseline analyses (67.2%), 61 longitudinal cohorts (20.2%), 35 case-control studies (11.6%) (p. 9 of the accepted manuscript). Study-level characteristics are in Supplemental file 3 (not read).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Figure 1 counts 1,015 full texts excluded and 98 articles excluded after data extraction; most of the reasons are clipped in the printed figure (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed literature only; English-language keywords in mostly English-language databases, which the authors say may have caused regional bias; single-reviewer screening and extraction with partial duplicate checks. Crack use was usually a secondary covariate in studies with other aims, and the samples were mostly marginalized, high-risk populations (people who inject drugs, sex workers, homeless people, pregnant women attending clinics), largely in the US (pp. 9, 22 of the accepted manuscript).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used, mostly self-reported crack use; definitions and timing of use in the primary studies are in Supplemental file 3 (not read).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mostly any crack use against none. Frequency, dose or duration appear only in the narrative synthesis (for example, no association of HIV seroprevalence with dose, frequency, duration or persistence of crack use among people using crack; p. 13 of the accepted manuscript). Route is smoking by definition; injection by the same people is not separated in the pooled analyses.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled at review level: the pooled odds ratios are mostly crude, and adjustment for other drug use exists only where a primary study adjusted (for the maternal outcomes, one study adjusted for alcohol and tobacco, p. 11). Within drug-using populations crack use was not consistently associated with HIV, hepatitis C or sexually transmitted infections (pp. 12–14).

comparison.controls: Within each primary study, people not using crack, described for the meta-analyses as people not using drugs or the general population; HIV seroprevalence was also pooled separately within men, women, transgender women, female sex workers, pregnant women and men who have sex with men. Some pooled control groups were themselves high-risk populations (for example youth living with HIV in Anaya et al., 2005, removed in a sensitivity analysis; p. 11 of the accepted manuscript).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. One HIV sensitivity analysis is restricted to age-adjusted estimates (19 studies).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressable from the pooled data; the authors note that with cross-sectional data health problems may precede crack use, and that marginalization may drive both crack use and outcomes (pp. 21–23 of the accepted manuscript).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Often unknown or present in the control groups; the comparison is crack use against no crack use, not against no drug use, in many studies.

outcomes.instruments: Primary-study measures: HIV seroconversion and seroprevalence, hepatitis B and C serology, sexually transmitted infections, tuberculosis, mental-health diagnoses or screens (including the MINI for depression), birth outcomes from records, experienced sexual assault and violence, mortality and others; listed per study in Supplemental file 3 (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary studies were not appraised for risk of bias; sample size, diagnostic tools and control-group composition were extracted as bias indicators, and the body of evidence for selected outcomes was graded A (conclusive) to E (no or insufficient evidence), grades assigned by one author and checked by an independent reviewer (pp. 8–9 of the accepted manuscript; Table 3, pp. 78–81).
outcomes.operationalization: A health outcome is any change in health status measurable or diagnosable compatibly with ICD-10, from records, tests or self-report (p. 6). Associations were summarized as pooled odds ratios, calculated by the reviewers from 2×2 data where a study gave none, or narratively as positive, null or mixed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 28 pooled estimates in Table 2 (described as 24 meta-analyses) plus narrative comparisons for many more outcomes.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening was by the lead author, with 500 of 4,700 titles and abstracts (84.4% agreement) and 44 full texts (81.8%) screened in duplicate; extraction by the lead author with 39 articles extracted in duplicate (86.9% agreement) (p. 9 of the accepted manuscript).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled odds ratios (Stata 14.1); I² given only in the printed forest plots and some text; no tau², no prediction intervals; raw totals only in Figures 2–4. Table 2 (pp. 73–77 of the accepted manuscript): HIV seroconversion 5.05 (2.16–11.80), 3 cohorts, I²=0%, all odds ratios calculated by the reviewers, 24/920 seroconversions with crack use vs 9/1517 without (Figure 2); HIV seroprevalence 2.94 (2.19–3.97), 29 studies; age-adjusted estimates only 3.16 (2.39–4.19), 19; men 3.09 (2.06–4.64), 7; women 3.55 (1.85–6.80), 16; transgender women 2.07 (1.35–3.17), 3; female sex workers 3.89 (2.14–7.08), 4; pregnant women 9.52 (3.86–23.51), 5; men who have sex with men 1.49 (0.44–5.01), 3, not significant. Sexually transmitted infections 2.59 (1.54–4.53), 3; syphilis 4.52 (2.69–7.59), 4; trichomonas 2.04 (1.25–3.31), 3; gonorrhoea 1.99 (0.62–6.39), 4, not significant. Hepatitis C 2.92 (2.50–3.40), 6; without one cohort study 2.25 (1.62–3.14), 5. General mental-health problems 2.51 (1.89–3.32), 3; suicidal ideation 3.66 (2.50–5.36), 4; depression 1.92 (0.93–3.95), 7, not significant, I²=89.3%; depression diagnosed with the MINI 4.52 (1.13–18.03), 3; by other methods 1.08 (0.63–1.86), 4; anxiety 1.19 (0.81–1.76), 5. Fetal growth restriction 2.30 (1.91–2.78), 8 studies, I²=65.9% (Figure 3); placental abruption 2.23 (1.24–4.02), 3; microcephaly 4.87 (2.13–11.12), 3; birth at 37 weeks or earlier 1.82 (1.01–3.27), 5; low 5-minute Apgar 1.37 (0.90–2.09), 3, not significant. Experienced sexual assault 4.17 (3.01–5.78), I²=0%, seven cross-sectional estimates (Figure 4); exposure to violence and physical abuse 2.06 (1.61–2.62), 3.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Pooled estimates mix crude odds ratios, many calculated by the reviewers, with adjusted ones; for the maternal outcomes only Sprauve et al. (1997) contributed adjusted estimates (pp. 10–11 of the accepted manuscript).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42016035486, cited as Butler et al. (2016), that is after the initial search of October 2015; the protocol was not read and the paper reports no comparison with it and no deviations. Reported according to PRISMA (2009 flow diagram).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only three of the forest plots are printed (Figures 2–4); the others are in a supplement (not read) and the funnel plots are not printed. Sensitivity analyses on heterogeneity are 'data not shown'. Cardiovascular and respiratory results appear only in Supplemental file 5 and as grades in Table 3. No absolute risks are reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Most pools contain 3–5 studies; the HIV seroconversion pool rests on 33 seroconversions in all; the authors note that few studies were available for the funnel plots.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against people not using crack in the same studies, crack use was associated with about 2–5 times the odds of HIV, hepatitis C and several sexually transmitted infections, of some maternal and neonatal outcomes, and of experienced sexual or physical violence, mostly in crude estimates from cross-sectional studies of high-risk populations; associations with depression (overall) and anxiety were not significant; within drug-using populations crack use was not consistently associated with HIV, hepatitis C or sexually transmitted infections; comparisons of crack with other cocaine use were mixed and not pooled. The authors' own grading gives no outcome grade A (conclusive): HIV, hepatitis C and sexually transmitted infections are graded B (substantial), all others C to E.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that "Conclusive evidence and meta-analyses showed positive associations" with HIV, hepatitis C and other infections (p. 2 of the accepted manuscript), while the Results, the Conclusions and Table 3 grade these as substantial (B) and no outcome is graded conclusive (pp. 19, 23, 78–81). The abstract's moderate evidence for violence concerns violence experienced; violence against others is graded D (limited) in Table 3. Results 3.3 lists cardiovascular disease among associations supported by moderate evidence (p. 19), but in Table 3 the only cardiovascular outcome graded C is a non-significant one (cardiovascular risk factors), and the significant ones are graded D. Mortality is graded C (moderate) in Table 3, while the abstract says evidence was insufficient for meta-analysis and the Discussion calls mortality data a major evidence gap (pp. 3, 20). Against this, the abstract's conclusion and the Discussion state plainly that causality is unclear and that crack is unlikely to be a direct cause of infections or violence (pp. 3, 21).

timeline.event: Gawin and Kleber's treatment-sample study is among the five studies reporting no difference between crack and other cocaine use for several psychiatric diagnoses, and among the 12 with mixed results (p. 16 of the accepted manuscript)
Narrative review comparing crack with cocaine hydrochloride; cited here as background on the emergence of crack and its distinct pharmacology and routes
US household survey of people who had just started cocaine; included in this review's narrative comparison of crack with other cocaine use, which it calls mixed
This review, described by its authors as the first comprehensive systematic review of health outcomes associated with crack use

replication.where_it_stands: In the sources read for this round, the only systematic review with meta-analyses of crack-specific health outcomes. Its pooled odds ratios describe crude associations between crack use and infections, maternal outcomes and victimization in high-risk populations up to 2016, not effects of crack and not differences from powder cocaine; the authors themselves place most of the risk in behaviours and environments. Primary studies central to the cocaine page (Chen and Anthony, 2004; Gawin and Kleber, 1986) are inside its narrative synthesis, so claims must not count them as independent support.

funding.funder: In part the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) for the Ontario Canadian Research Initiative in Substance Misuse (CRISM) Node Team (Grant #SMN-139 150) and a CIHR/Public Health Agency of Canada Research Chair awarded to Fischer; the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Role of Funding Sources, p. 24 of the accepted manuscript).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (Conflict of Interest, p. 24 of the accepted manuscript).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and the University of Toronto, and the Technische Universität Dresden. Studies co-authored by the review authors are among those synthesized (Fischer et al., 2005 and 2006; Wild et al., 2005, with Fischer and Rehm; DeBeck et al., 2009, with Fischer); no procedure for this is described. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use crack, powder cocaine or no cocaine, recruited from comparable populations, with injection, sexual behaviour, sex work, housing and other drug use measured over time, analysed with adjusted models for incident HIV, hepatitis C, sexually transmitted infections, violence and mortality; and an updated systematic review that appraises each study's risk of bias, pools adjusted estimates separately from crude ones, does not count the same infants twice, and compares crack with powder cocaine directly.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people using crack), exposure, comparator (no use or different levels) and outcomes (any ICD-10-compatible health outcome) are specified, with eligible designs (pp. 5–7 of the accepted manuscript).
PROSPERO CRD42016035486, cited as 2016, after the initial search of October 2015; the protocol was not read, and no deviations are reported or discussed.
Case-control, cohort and cross-sectional designs are listed without a reason for the choice (p. 6).

Six databases with strategies in Supplemental file 1, reference lists, no language or date limits, search completed within a year of acceptance; the restriction to peer-reviewed work is justified by resource constraints; no grey literature, registries or expert contact.
One screener, with duplicate samples reaching the 80% agreement AMSTAR 2 accepts: 84.4% for 500 titles and abstracts, 81.8% for 44 full texts (p. 9).
One extractor; 39 articles extracted in duplicate with 86.9% agreement (p. 9), meeting AMSTAR 2's sample criterion.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only counts by reason in Figure 1, most of them clipped in the printed figure; no list in the article, and no supplement is described as containing one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article gives only article counts by chapter (Table 1) and reference lists by pool (Table 2); study descriptions are in Supplemental file 3, not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias tool; sample size, diagnostic tools and control-group composition were extracted, and the grading rates the body of evidence, not individual studies (pp. 8–9).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random effects, but mostly crude odds ratios (many calculated by the reviewers) are pooled with adjusted ones without justification, designs are combined, and in the fetal growth restriction pool three studies each contribute two outcomes from the same infants, so the overall estimate counts 580 exposed and 3,269 control infants twice (Figure 3; editors' arithmetic).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses by design, population and reported versus calculated odds ratios (mostly data not shown), but none by risk of bias, which was not assessed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion and Limitations address reverse causation in cross-sectional data and confounding by marginalization and risk environments, and state that crack is not a plausible direct cause of infections or violence (pp. 21–23). A close call: no study-level appraisal underlies this, and the abstract calls the infection evidence conclusive.

I² reported for the printed pools and in the text (0% to 89%); subgroup pools by population and diagnostic method; sensitivity analyses described (data not shown); pools with high heterogeneity flagged for caution (pp. 10–11, 22–23).
Funnel plots (not printed) were examined and possible publication bias in the maternal and sexually transmitted infection pools is reported, with the caveat that each had few studies (p. 11).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the funders' role are stated and no conflict is declared; the inclusion of the authors' own studies is not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 depends on Supplemental file 3, which was not read; it cannot change the result. Three critical items are not met (7, no list of excluded studies; 9, no risk-of-bias assessment of the included studies; 11, crude and adjusted estimates pooled without justification and correlated estimates from the same infants pooled as independent), items 2 and 4 are partly met and items 13 and 15 are met, so AMSTAR 2 confidence is critically low. The review is broad, registered, searches six databases without language limits and is candid about causality, but its pooled odds ratios are crude associations in selected, high-risk populations. It may be cited for which outcomes have been studied, for the crude associations with infections, maternal outcomes and experienced violence (as associations against people not using crack), and for its finding that within drug-using populations crack use is not consistently associated with HIV or hepatitis C; not for causal effects, for differences between crack and powder cocaine, for mortality, or as conclusive evidence.

key_findings.finding: 4,700 records were screened (5,643 from databases and 827 from reference lists, less 1,770 duplicates), 1,415 full texts assessed, 400 articles extracted, 302 included and 79 used in meta-analyses.

Included articles came mostly from the US (206, 68.2%), Brazil (32, 10.6%) and Canada (22, 7.3%); 203 (67.2%) were cross-sectional or cohort-baseline analyses, 61 (20.2%) longitudinal cohorts and 35 (11.6%) case-control studies.

Six databases were searched in October 2015 and again in October 2016, peer-reviewed studies only, without language or date limits; crack use meant crack, freebase or alkaloid cocaine, or smoked cocaine, with mixed groups included if at least 75% used crack; meta-analyses were run only where at least three studies had comparable control groups of people not using drugs or the general population.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Search Strategy and Selection Criteria, 1st, 4th and 5th paragraphs (pp. 5–7); 2.2, 4th paragraph (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: HIV seroconversion: pooled odds ratio 5.05 (2.16–11.80), I²=0%, from three cohorts whose odds ratios were all calculated by the reviewers: 24 of 920 people using crack seroconverted against 9 of 1,517 controls. Table 2 labels this pool HIV seroconversion in women; Figure 2 and the text do not.
key_findings.note: Figure 2 is an image without a text layer; its values were read on the rendered page, so a mechanical number search of the text will not find them. Single studies: Chirgwin (1999) 4.61 (0.47–45.69); Seage (2001) 3.76 (0.84–16.92); Novak (2013) 6.13 (1.94–19.40). 33 seroconversions in all; crude estimates.

key_findings.finding: HIV seroprevalence, crack use against no crack use: 2.94 (2.19–3.97), 29 studies; restricted to age-adjusted estimates 3.16 (2.39–4.19), 19 studies; within men 3.09 (2.06–4.64), women 3.55 (1.85–6.80), transgender women 2.07 (1.35–3.17), female sex workers 3.89 (2.14–7.08) and pregnant women 9.52 (3.86–23.51); men who have sex with men 1.49 (0.44–5.01), not significant.

In the narrative synthesis, crack use was not consistently associated with HIV seroconversion or seroprevalence among people who inject drugs or other drug-using populations, or with HIV among other high-risk groups; HIV seroprevalence showed no association with dose, frequency, duration or persistence of crack use; and crack use was not consistently associated with sexually transmitted infections or hepatitis C in drug-using populations.

Sexually transmitted infections 2.59 (1.54–4.53), 3 studies; syphilis 4.52 (2.69–7.59), 4; trichomonas 2.04 (1.25–3.31), 3; gonorrhoea 1.99 (0.62–6.39), 4, not significant; hepatitis C 2.92 (2.50–3.40), 6 studies, and 2.25 (1.62–3.14) without one cohort study.

Mental health, crack use against no crack use: general mental-health problems 2.51 (1.89–3.32), 3 studies; suicidal ideation 3.66 (2.50–5.36), 4; depression 1.92 (0.93–3.95), 7, not significant, I²=89.3%; depression diagnosed with the MINI 4.52 (1.13–18.03), 3, and by other methods 1.08 (0.63–1.86), 4; anxiety 1.19 (0.81–1.76), 5, not significant; I² at most 5.5% for the other mental-health pools; estimates mix crude and adjusted odds ratios.
key_findings.note: Table 2 marks anxiety as a positive association although its interval includes 1; the text calls it not significant (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Comparisons of people using crack with people using other cocaine are described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies, including Chen and Anthony, 2004, and Gawin and Kleber, 1986), and as showing no difference for ADHD, antisocial personality disorder, bipolar disorders, dysthymia, eating disorders, mania, obsessive-compulsive disorder, psychotic symptoms, PTSD or substance-induced disorders (5 studies); among people using cocaine, crack use went with anorexia and insomnia in one study and with less suicidal ideation in another. None of these comparisons was pooled or tested.

Maternal crack use against none: fetal growth restriction 2.30 (1.91–2.78), 8 studies, I²=65.9%; placental abruption 2.23 (1.24–4.02), 3; microcephaly 4.87 (2.13–11.12), 3; birth at 37 weeks or earlier 1.82 (1.01–3.27), 5; low 5-minute Apgar 1.37 (0.90–2.09), 3, not significant. These rest mostly on crude odds ratios, and the authors note the associations became less clear when trimester-specific use and tobacco and alcohol were controlled.
key_findings.note: Figure 3 is an image without a text layer; its values (I² 65.9%, weights, single studies) were read on the page rendered at 300 dpi. In Figure 3 (overall 2.30, 1.91–2.77) three of the eight studies contribute both a birth-weight and a small-for-gestational-age estimate from the same infants (see reporting issues); the only adjusted estimates, Sprauve et al. (1997), carry 55% of the weight and are the smallest in each subgroup (1.59 and 1.70).

key_findings.finding: Experienced sexual assault 4.17 (3.01–5.78), I²=0%, from seven cross-sectional estimates (202 of 1,504 people using crack against 279 of 3,464 controls); exposure to violence and physical abuse 2.06 (1.61–2.62), 3 studies. Violence against others was associated with crack use only in some groups and is graded D; one study found more violence toward others among people smoking crack than among people snorting cocaine, but not more than among people injecting it.
key_findings.note: Figure 4 is an image without a text layer; the seven estimates and totals were read on the rendered page. Table 2 gives 4 studies for the sexual-assault pool and Table 3 gives 6 articles (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality: higher than in the general population in two studies and among hospitalized stroke patients in one, but not among people with HIV or people who inject drugs; not pooled; graded C (moderate) in Table 3, while the Discussion calls mortality data a major evidence gap.

Grades (Table 3): HIV, hepatitis C and sexually transmitted infections B (substantial); tuberculosis, progression to AIDS, fetal growth restriction, premature birth, microcephaly, placental abruption, sexual and physical assault, mortality, and the non-significant cardiovascular risk factors and low Apgar C (moderate); depression, anxiety and dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances D (limited), all non-significant; no outcome graded A (conclusive).
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Quality of Evidence (p. 19); Table 3 and its legend (pp. 78–81)
key_findings.note: The dependence row (5 articles, not significant, grade D) lists binge use of crack as a possible pathway to dependence; it is not graded as a crack–powder comparison.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that crack is not a plausible direct cause of sexually transmitted infections, HIV, hepatitis C or violence, but a facilitator or marker of risk behaviours and environments, and that for mental health it is unclear whether crack use is a cause, a consequence or comorbid.

Funnel plots suggested possible publication bias in the maternal and sexually transmitted infection pools, each with few studies; heterogeneity was considerable for HIV, depression, fetal growth restriction, premature birth and sexually transmitted infections; sensitivity analyses (data not shown) found no difference between cross-sectional and case-control studies or between reported and calculated odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says conclusive evidence and meta-analyses showed associations with HIV, hepatitis C and other infections, but Table 3 grades these outcomes B (substantial) and grades nothing A (conclusive), and the Results and Conclusions also say substantial.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must use the review's own grade (substantial), not 'conclusive'. The version of record was not read and may differ.

reporting_issues.issue: Results 3.3 lists cardiovascular disease among associations supported by moderate evidence, but in Table 3 the only cardiovascular outcome graded C is the non-significant 'cardiovascular risk factors'; high blood pressure, hypoxic brain lesions and overall heart problems are graded D and stroke E.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review cannot be cited for moderate evidence of a cardiovascular association.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks anxiety as a positive association (OR 1.19, 0.81–1.76) although the interval includes 1; the text and Table 3 call it not significant.
The experienced-sexual-assault pool is given as 4 studies in Table 2, while Figure 4 pools seven estimates (matching the seven references listed in Table 2) and Table 3 counts 6 articles.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pool should be described from Figure 4: seven cross-sectional estimates, 202 of 1,504 against 279 of 3,464.

reporting_issues.issue: In the fetal growth restriction meta-analysis (Figure 3, an image without a text layer), Cherukuri (1988), Sprauve (1997) and Richardson (1999) each contribute two estimates, birth weight of 2500 g or less and small for gestational age, from the same infants. The overall upper limit is 2.77 in Figure 3 and 2.78 in Table 2. Editors' arithmetic: the overall pool, 1,836 exposed and 8,139 control infants in the figure, counts 580 exposed and 3,269 control infants twice. The control proportion small for gestational age in Fulroth (1989), 12 of 985 (1.2%), is far below what a 10th-centile definition would give; the definitions used are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The overall interval is too narrow; the subgroup pools (birth weight 2.37, 1.84–3.07; small for gestational age 2.22, 1.68–2.92) are the defensible figures. The only adjusted estimates (Sprauve, 1.59 and 1.70) are the smallest in their subgroups, in line with the authors' remark that associations became less clear with adjustment.

reporting_issues.issue: HIV seroconversion is labelled 'in women' in Table 2 but not in Figure 2, the Results or the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: The population of the 5.05 estimate is unclear from the article; claims should not attach it to women without checking the three primary cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: Mortality is graded C (moderate) in Table 3, while the abstract says the evidence was insufficient for meta-analysis and the Discussion calls mortality data a major evidence gap.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mortality grade should not be cited as moderate evidence of an effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed PRISMA diagram clips most exclusion reasons; they survive only in the PDF's hidden text layer, which lists four reasons for the 98 articles excluded after extraction (35, 25, 18 and 18). Editors' arithmetic: these sum to 96.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two exclusions are unexplained, and the reasons cannot be read on the printed figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 counts articles by ICD-10 chapter or category for the 302 included articles, and the text gives design counts of 203, 61 and 35. Editors' arithmetic: Table 1 sums to 297, fewer than 302 although an article can appear in more than one category, and the design counts sum to 299.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; at least five included articles are not accounted for in Table 1 and three in the design breakdown.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 sends readers to 'Supplemental file 2' for the forest plots, whereas the text places the remaining forest plots in Supplemental file 4 and the grading criteria in Supplemental file 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Supplement references cannot be relied on as printed.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cocaine/Butler_2017_CrackHealthOutcomesSRMA.pdf: the accepted manuscript (unedited), 82 PDF pages, an unnumbered Elsevier cover page and then pages printed 'Page 1 of 81' to 'Page 81 of 81'; anchors cite these printed manuscript pages ('p. N of the accepted manuscript'; PDF page = printed page + 1); the version of record (Drug Alcohol Depend 2017;180:401–416) was not read. All text, the reference list, Tables 1–3 and Figures 1–4 read, the tables and figures on pages rendered at 150 dpi and Figure 3 also at 300 dpi; Supplemental files 1–5 (search strings, extraction template and further methods; grading criteria; study tables; remaining forest plots; other outcomes including cardiovascular and respiratory) are not on file and were not read, and the funnel plots are not printed.
